newsitem.title: UK: Analysts see Russian diamond row blowing over.
newsitem.headline: Analysts see Russian diamond row blowing over.

text.p: Harsh words in the world of diamonds have caused a stir among investors, but the prospect of a price war between Russia and South Africa's diamond giant De Beers are slim, analysts said on Thursday.
They believe common sense will prevail over any short-term greed and see the basic structure of diamond trading remaining intact.

But even if the rift between De Beers and Russia turns really sour, industry watchers see Russian mines, Australian producers and Indian polishers suffering more than De Beers, whose shares fell sharply on the Johannesburg exchange.

"That (a price war) would hurt De Beers, but it wouldn't hurt them as much as Russia, and it would certainly kick Australia's Argyle in the teeth and the country that would come out the worst would be India," said Peter Davey at brokers Lehman Brothers.
Argyle cut ties with de Beers in June and now independently sells its low-grade diamonds, mainly polished in India.

But the doom scenario is unlikely to become reality as cash-strapped Russia stands to gain more in the long-term if it retains a friendly relationship with De Beers, which controls about 75 percent of the world diamond trade.
"Price instability is in nobody's interest," said Marc Cockle, editor of trade magazine Diamond International.
Such soothing comments come after De Beers abruptly spoke out on Wednesday, saying it would stop doing business on current terms in 1997 if Russia did not approve a new sales pact.

The pact has for years been a bone of contention between Russia and De Beers, which has had an iron grip on trading in rough stones since the 1930s through its Central Selling Organisation (CSO). Most of the diamonds sold by the CSO to polishing centres such as Antwerp, Tel Aviv and Bombay, come from De Beers itself, which is responsible for about 50 percent of world production.
The rest comes from other producers of which Russia is the most important.
De Beers and Russia have been reviewing their relationship in the past two years as a five-year sales pact expired end-1995. The problem was that this pact was not very effective.
Differences in interpretation allowed Russia to sell many diamonds outside the CSO directly onto world markets.

Russia and De Beers seemed close to a new deal when they signed a memorandum of understanding in February. De Beers then agreed a final contract in September with Almazy-Rossii Sakha (ARS), Russia's main diamond producer.

But the Russian government has since refused to approve the deal as a battle continues over control of diamond revenues. Meanwhile the previous pact, which obliges de Beers to buy about 95 percent of Russian production, has remained operational.
The South African giant said yesterday that it will not stick to that agreement any more from January 1.

This will give De Beers the freedom to buy any quantity of Russian stones it wants, but it also increases the risk of more diamonds being sold by Russia directly to polishing centres, which might lead to price pressure.
This, however, would ruin Russia's own market in the long term and that, analysts believe, would not be desirable.
An extra reason not to upset diamond markets would be ARS' need to secure loans from western banks for necessary investment for mine maintenance needed to keep up production.
ARS is known to be negotiating a $500 million package with NatWest Markets. But the British bank could be reluctant to do business if ARS takes on giant De Beers, industry watchers said.
"I would presume that the Russians are sensible enough to see that if they destroy the market there is no way that they'll get a loan," said Charles Kernot at Paribas Markets.
"They would end up with no export revenue from diamonds by the end of the century," he added.

If Russia starts a price war nonetheless, analysts forecast it will be fought largely in the lower segment of the market as Russia has recently been less involved in the far more profitable big gem business.
While demand for large stones is booming, prices for smaller diamonds have slipped slightly since the summer when Argyle, the world's biggest producer of small stones, left the CSO.
But Cockle of Diamond International said the Indian polishers have little reason to worry, as the Argyle pull-out did not result in the havoc feared by many.

He similarly played down uncertainties over the new relationship between De Beers and Russia: "There is not going to be any increased supply of diamonds, it is just a different arrangement of selling them."
